170	  \uses{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   171	
   172	  If \(1\le r\le g\), there is a dense open subset of \(C^{(r)}\) on which
   173	  \(h^0(D)=1\).  Thus the fibres of \(f^{(r)}\) over this open consist of one
   174	  geometric point.
   175	\end{lemma}
   176	
   177	\begin{proof}
   178	  If \(h^1(D)>0\), Serre duality identifies
   179	  \[
   180	    H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(D+Q))^\vee
   181	  \]
   182	  with the subspace of \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\) consisting of
   183	  differentials that vanish at \(Q\).  Outside the common zero locus of a
   184	  basis of this latter space,
   185	  adding \(Q\) lowers \(h^1\) by exactly one.  Starting with the zero
   186	  divisor, for which \(h^1=g\), and repeating this argument \(r\) times
   187	  gives a dense open subset of \(C^r\) on which
   188	  \(h^1(P_1+\cdots+P_r)=g-r\).  Riemann--Roch then gives
   189	  \[
   190	    h^0(P_1+\cdots+P_r)
   191	      =r+1-g+(g-r)=1.
   192	  \]
   193	  Intersecting its finitely many translates under \(S_r\) gives a dense
   194	  symmetric open with the same property.  Its image in the finite quotient
   195	  \(C^{(r)}\) is the complement of the image of its closed invariant
   196	  complement, hence is open and dense.
   197	  Since the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through \(D\) is \(|D|\), it is a single
   198	  point there.
   199	\end{proof}
   200	
   201	\begin{lemma}
   202	  [One-forms pulled back by the Abel--Jacobi map]
   203	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   204	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   205	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   206	
   207	  Pullback by \(\iota_{P_0}\) is an isomorphism
   208	  \[
   209	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0(C,\Omega_C^1).
   210	  \]
   211	\end{lemma}
   212	
   213	\begin{proof}
   214	  \uses{thm:pic0_tangent_space_iso}
   215	  Translation identifies global one-forms on the smooth group scheme \(J\)
   216	  with the cotangent space at its identity.  The tangent-space description
   217	  of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) identifies the tangent space at the identity with
   218	  \(H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\), whose dual is
   219	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\) by Serre duality.  Under these identifications, the
   220	  differential of the moduli class
   221	  \(Q\mapsto[\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0)]\) is the boundary class of the moving
   222	  point; its dual is evaluation of differentials.  Thus the induced map on
   223	  cotangent spaces, and hence the displayed pullback map, is the identity
   224	  under the canonical identifications.
   225	\end{proof}
   226	
   227	\begin{lemma}
   228	  [Dimension of the Jacobian]
   229	  \label{lem:jacobian_dimension}
   230	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107}
   231	
   232	  The Jacobian has dimension \(g\).
   233	\end{lemma}
   234	
   235	\begin{proof}
   236	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms, thm:pic0_smooth}
   237	  Since \(J\) is smooth, its dimension is the dimension of its cotangent
   238	  space at the identity.  Translation identifies that cotangent space with
   239	  the global one-forms on \(J\).  By
   240	  \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, this space is isomorphic to
   241	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), whose dimension is the genus \(g\).
   242	\end{proof}
   243	
   244	\begin{proposition}
   245	  [Differentials on a symmetric power]
   246	  \label{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   247	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   248	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve,
   249	    def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   250	
   251	  Pullback by \(f^{(r)}\) is an isomorphism
   252	  \[
   253	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}
   254	    H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega_{C^{(r)}}^1).
   255	  \]
   256	  Under the canonical identification of either side with
   257	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), the form corresponding to \(\omega\) vanishes at
   258	  an effective divisor \(D\) if and only if
   259	  \(\operatorname{div}(\omega)\ge D\).
   260	\end{proposition}
   261	
   262	\begin{proof}
   263	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   264	  A global one-form on \(C^r\) is a sum of pullbacks from the factors.
   265	  Hence the invariant forms are exactly
   266	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\), with \(\omega\in H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\).
   267	  The quotient map \(\pi_r\) is separable, so pullback embeds
   268	  \(H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)\) into this invariant subspace.  The composite
   269	  \[
   270	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\longrightarrow H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)
   271	      \longrightarrow H^0(C^r,\Omega^1)^{S_r}
   272	  \]
   273	  is the pullback by the sum of the \(r\) copies of the Abel--Jacobi map.
   274	  By \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, it sends a form to
   275	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\) and is an isomorphism.  Consequently both arrows
   276	  in the display are isomorphisms.
   277	
   278	  It remains to identify vanishing at a divisor.  First take \(D=rQ\),
   279	  choose a parameter \(X\) at \(Q\), and write
   280	  \(\omega=(a_0+a_1X+\cdots)dX\).  In the completed local ring of
   281	  \(C^{(r)}\) at \(D\), use the elementary symmetric functions
   282	  \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r\) in local parameters
   283	  \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\), and put
   284	  \(\tau_j=\sum_iX_i^j\,dX_i\).  The identities
   285	  \[
   286	    \sigma_m\tau_0-\sigma_{m-1}\tau_1+\cdots+(-1)^m\tau_m
   287	      =d\sigma_{m+1}
   288	      \qquad(0\le m<r)
   289	  \]
   290	  show that \(\tau_0,\ldots,\tau_{r-1}\) form a basis of the cotangent
   291	  module.  The descended form is \(\sum_{j\ge0}a_j\tau_j\), so it
   292	  vanishes at \(D\) exactly when
   293	  \(a_0=\cdots=a_{r-1}=0\), equivalently when
   294	  \(\operatorname{ord}_Q(\omega)\ge r\).  The same calculation in the
   295	  completed local product for
   296	  \(D=\sum_Q n_QQ\) gives the stated criterion.
   297	\end{proof}
   298	
   299	\begin{lemma}
   300	  [Tangent sequence of the canonical symmetric-power map]
   301	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact}
   302	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   303	  \uses{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   304	
   305	  Let \(F=|D|\) be the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through an effective divisor
   306	  \(D\), and put \(a=f^{(r)}(D)\).  The sequence
   307	  \[
   308	    0\longrightarrow T_DF\longrightarrow T_DC^{(r)}
   309	      \xrightarrow{\,d f^{(r)}_D\,}T_aJ
   310	  \]
   311	  is exact.  In particular, if \(h^0(D)=1\), then
   312	  \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is injective.
   313	\end{lemma}
   314	
   315	\begin{proof}
   316	  \uses{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   317	  The first arrow is injective because the fibre is a closed subscheme, and
   318	  its image lies in the kernel because \(f^{(r)}\) is constant on the
   319	  fibre.  By \cref{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}, the annihilator
   320	  in \(T_aJ^\vee\) of the image of \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is
   321	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\).  Serre duality therefore gives
   322	  \[
   323	    \dim\ker(d f^{(r)}_D)=r-g+h^1(D).
   324	  \]
   325	  The fibre \(F\) is the projective space of effective divisors in the
   326	  complete linear system, so it is smooth of dimension \(h^0(D)-1\).
   327	  Thus \(\dim T_DF=\dim|D|=h^0(D)-1\), and Riemann--Roch says
   328	  \(h^0(D)-1=r-g+h^1(D)\).  The included subspaces have the same
   329	  dimension, proving exactness.  When \(h^0(D)=1\), this dimension is zero.
   330	\end{proof}

1	% source: J. S. Milne, "Abelian Varieties" (course notes), v2.00, 2008, www.jmilne.org
     2	% pdf_page: 0100
     3	% doc_page: 94 (Chapter III, Section 3, "The symmetric powers of a curve"; Propositions 3.1 and 3.2)
     4	% retrieved: 2026-06-17
     5	% transcribed_by: Codex GPT-5 (vision, rendered at 200dpi via pdftoppm)
     6	
     7	% [running head: CHAPTER III. JACOBIAN VARIETIES, page 94]
     8	
     9	\section*{3 \quad The symmetric powers of a curve}
    10	
    11	Both in order to understand the structure of the Jacobian, and as an aid in
    12	its construction, we shall need to study the symmetric powers of $C$.
    13	
    14	For any variety $V$, the symmetric group $S_r$ on $r$ letters acts on the
    15	product of $r$ copies $V^r$ of $V$ by permuting the factors, and we want to
    16	define the $r$th symmetric power $V^{(r)}$ of $V$ to be the quotient
    17	$S_r \backslash V^r$. The next proposition demonstrates the existence of
    18	$V^{(r)}$ and lists its main properties.
    19	
    20	A morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ is said to be \textit{symmetric} if
    21	$\varphi\sigma = \varphi$ for all $\sigma$ in $S_r$.
    22	
    23	\paragraph{Proposition 3.1.}
    24	\textit{Let $V$ be a variety over $k$. Then there exists a variety $V^{(r)}$
    25	and a symmetric morphism $\pi \colon V^r \to V^{(r)}$ having the following
    26	properties:}
    27	
    28	\begin{enumerate}
    29	\item[(a)] \textit{as a topological space, $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is the quotient
    30	of $V^r$ by $S_r$;}
    31	\item[(b)] \textit{for any open affine subset $U$ of $V$, $U^{(r)}$ is an
    32	open affine subset of $V^{(r)}$ and}
    33	\[
    34	  \Gamma(U^{(r)}, \mathcal{O}_{V^{(r)}})
    35	  = \Gamma(U^r, \mathcal{O}_{V^r})^{S_r}
    36	\]
    37	\textit{(set of elements fixed by the action of $S_r$).}
    38	\end{enumerate}
    39	
    40	\textit{The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ has the following universal property:
    41	every symmetric $k$-morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ factors uniquely
    42	through $\pi$.}
    43	
    44	\textit{The map $\pi$ is finite, surjective, and separable.}
    45	
    46	\paragraph{Proof.}
    47	If $V$ is affine, say $V = \operatorname{Specm}(A)$, define $V^{(r)}$ to be
    48	$\operatorname{Specm}((A \otimes_k \cdots \otimes_k A)^{S_r})$. In the
    49	general case, write $V$ as a union $\bigcup U_i$ of open affines, and construct
    50	$V$ by patching together the $U_i^{(r)}$. See Mumford 1970, II, \S 7, p66,
    51	and III, \S 11, p112, for the details. \hfill $\square$
    52	
    53	The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is uniquely determined up to a unique isomorphism
    54	by its universal property. It is called the $r$th \textit{symmetric power} of
    55	$V$.
    56	
    57	\paragraph{Proposition 3.2.}
    58	\textit{The symmetric power $C^{(r)}$ of a nonsingular curve is nonsingular.}
    59	
    60	\paragraph{Proof.}
    61	We may assume that $k$ is algebraically closed. The most likely candidate for
    62	a singular point on $C^{(r)}$ is the image $Q$ of a fixed point
    63	$(P, \ldots, P)$ of $S_r$ on $C^r$, where $P$ is a closed point of $C$. The
    64	completion $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_P$ of the local ring at $P$ is isomorphic to
    65	$k[[X]]$, and so
    66	\[
    67	  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{(P,\ldots,P)}
    68	  \approx k[[X]] \widehat{\otimes} \cdots \widehat{\otimes} k[[X]]
    69	  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]].
    70	\]
    71	It follows that
    72	$\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r}$, where $S_r$
    73	acts by permuting the variables. The fundamental theorem on symmetric
    74	functions says that, over any ring, a symmetric polynomial can be expressed
    75	as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions
    76	$\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r$. This implies that
    77	\[
    78	  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r} = k[[\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r]],
    79	\]
    80	which is regular, and so $Q$ is nonsingular.
    81	
    82	For a general point $Q = \pi(P, P, \ldots, P', \ldots)$ with $P$ occurring
    83	$r'$ times, $P'$ occurring $r''$ times, and so on,
    84	\[
    85	  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q
    86	  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r'}]]^{S_{r'}} \widehat{\otimes}
    87	  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r''}]]^{S_{r''}} \widehat{\otimes} \cdots,
    88	\]
    89	which the same argument shows to be regular. \hfill $\square$

1	\chapter{The Albanese universal property of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\)}
     2	\label{chap:Albanese_AlbaneseUP}
     3	% archon:covers AlgebraicJacobian/Albanese/AlbaneseUP.lean
     4	
     5	Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(C\) be a smooth proper
     6	geometrically irreducible curve over \(k\), and let \(P_0\in C(k)\).  Write
     7	\(g\) for the genus of \(C\) and assume \(g>0\).  This chapter proves that
     8	the Abel--Jacobi map
     9	\[
    10	  \iota_{P_0}\colon C\longrightarrow \Pic^0_{C/k}
    11	\]
    12	is the Albanese morphism of the pointed curve \((C,P_0)\).  The proof uses
    13	the canonical map from the \(g\)-th symmetric power of \(C\) to its
    14	Jacobian.  In positive characteristic, generic injectivity of this map does
    15	not by itself imply birationality: a purely inseparable map may also have
    16	one geometric point in its generic fibre.  The differential calculation
    17	that excludes this possibility is therefore included explicitly.
    18	
    19	\section{The Jacobian and the Abel--Jacobi map}
    20	\label{sec:albaneseup_setup}
    21	
    22	The construction of the identity component of the Picard scheme gives
    23	\[
    24	  J:=\Pic^0_{C/k}.
    25	\]
    26	It is a group scheme by \cref{thm:pic0_group_structure}, smooth by
    27	\cref{thm:pic0_smooth}, proper by \cref{thm:pic0_proper}, and geometrically
    28	irreducible by \cref{thm:pic0_geom_irred}.
    29	
    30	\begin{definition}
    31	  [The Abel--Jacobi morphism]
    32	  \label{def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
    33	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107}
    34	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.abelJacobi}
    35	  \uses{def:pic_scheme, thm:pic0_group_structure}
    36	
    37	  The relative degree-zero line bundle associated with the rigidified
    38	  diagonal on \(C\times C\) defines a classifying morphism
    39	  \(\iota_{P_0}\colon C\to J\), called the \emph{Abel--Jacobi morphism}.
    40	\end{definition}
    41	
    42	\begin{lemma}
    43	  [Formula and basepoint of the Abel--Jacobi morphism]
    44	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism}
    45	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0110}
    46	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
    47	
    48	  There is a regular morphism
    49	  \[
    50	    \iota_{P_0}\colon C\longrightarrow J,
    51	    \qquad Q\longmapsto [\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0)],
    52	  \]
    53	  and \(\iota_{P_0}(P_0)=0_J\).
    54	\end{lemma}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  On \(C\times C\), viewed over the second factor, consider the
    58	  rigidified relative degree-zero line bundle represented by
    59	  \[
    60	    \mathcal O_{C\times C}
    61	      (\Delta-P_0\times C-C\times P_0).
    62	  \]
    63	  Its restriction over \(Q\in C(k)\), modulo a line bundle pulled back
    64	  from the base, is \(\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0)\).  The moduli property of
    65	  \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) therefore gives the displayed morphism.  At \(Q=P_0\)
    66	  the fibre is the trivial line bundle, whose class is the identity of
    67	  \(J\).
    68	\end{proof}
    69	
    70	\section{Symmetric powers and their canonical maps}
    71	\label{sec:albaneseup_symmetric_powers}
    72	
    73	\begin{definition}
    74	  [Symmetric power of a curve]
    75	  \label{def:symmetric_power_curve}
    76	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0100}
    77	
    78	  For \(r\ge 1\), the \emph{\(r\)-th symmetric power} \(C^{(r)}\) is the
    79	  quotient of \(C^r\) by permutation of the factors.  It is equipped with a
    80	  finite surjective morphism \(\pi_r\colon C^r\to C^{(r)}\).  Every
    81	  symmetric morphism from \(C^r\) to a \(k\)-scheme factors uniquely through
    82	  \(\pi_r\).
    83	\end{definition}
    84	
    85	\begin{definition}
    86	  [The symmetric-power carrier]
    87	  \label{def:symmetric_power_curve_carrier}
    88	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.SymmetricPower}
    89	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
    90	
    91	  The underlying \(k\)-scheme of \(C^{(r)}\) is denoted
    92	  \(\operatorname{SymmetricPower}(C,r)\).
    93	\end{definition}
    94	
    95	\begin{lemma}
    96	  [Nonsingularity of a symmetric power of a curve]
    97	  \label{lem:symmetric_power_nonsingular}
    98	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0100}
    99	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   100	
   101	  If \(C\) is nonsingular, then \(C^{(r)}\) is nonsingular.
   102	\end{lemma}
   103	
   104	\begin{proof}
   105	  At the image of \((Q,\ldots,Q)\), choose a parameter \(X\) at \(Q\).
   106	  The completed local ring of \(C^r\) is
   107	  \(k[[X_1,\ldots,X_r]]\), and the completed local ring of the quotient is
   108	  its invariant subring.  The fundamental theorem on symmetric functions
   109	  identifies this with
   110	  \(k[[\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r]]\), which is regular.  At a divisor with
   111	  several distinct support points, the completed local ring is the
   112	  completed tensor product of the corresponding invariant power-series
   113	  rings, and is again regular.
   114	\end{proof}
   115	
   116	\begin{definition}
   117	  [The symmetric sum morphism]
   118	  \label{def:symmetric_product_av_map}
   119	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerAVMap}
   120	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve_carrier}
   121	
   122	  For a morphism \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) to an abelian variety, denote the
   123	  induced morphism from the symmetric-power carrier by
   124	  \(\varphi^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\to A\).
   125	\end{definition}
   126	
   127	\begin{lemma}
   128	  [Symmetrisation of a morphism to an abelian variety]
   129	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_av_map}
   130	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   131	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve, def:symmetric_product_av_map}
   132	
   133	  Let \(A\) be an abelian variety and let \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) be a
   134	  morphism.  There is a unique morphism
   135	  \(\varphi^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\to A\) satisfying
   136	  \[
   137	    \varphi^{(r)}(P_1+\cdots+P_r)
   138	      =\varphi(P_1)+\cdots+\varphi(P_r).
   139	  \]
   140	\end{lemma}
   141	
   142	\begin{proof}
   143	  The morphism \(C^r\to A\) obtained by applying \(\varphi\) in every
   144	  coordinate and then adding is invariant under every permutation, because
   145	  the group law of \(A\) is commutative.  The universal property of
   146	  \(C^{(r)}\) gives the unique factorisation.
   147	\end{proof}
   148	
   149	\begin{definition}
   150	  [The canonical symmetric-power morphism to the Jacobian]
   151	  \label{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   152	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107}
   153	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerToJacobian}
   154	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism, def:symmetric_product_av_map}
   155	
   156	  Symmetrising \(\iota_{P_0}\) gives the canonical morphism
   157	  \[
   158	    f^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\longrightarrow J,
   159	    \qquad
   160	    D\longmapsto[\mathcal O_C(D-rP_0)].
   161	  \]
   162	  Its image is denoted \(W^r\).  The fibre through an effective divisor
   163	  \(D\) is its complete linear system \(|D|\).
   164	\end{definition}
   165	
   166	\begin{lemma}
   167	  [General divisors of degree at most the genus]
   168	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_general_divisor}
   169	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   170	  \uses{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   171	
   172	  If \(1\le r\le g\), there is a dense open subset of \(C^{(r)}\) on which
   173	  \(h^0(D)=1\).  Thus the fibres of \(f^{(r)}\) over this open consist of one
   174	  geometric point.
   175	\end{lemma}
   176	
   177	\begin{proof}
   178	  If \(h^1(D)>0\), Serre duality identifies
   179	  \[
   180	    H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(D+Q))^\vee
   181	  \]
   182	  with the subspace of \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\) consisting of
   183	  differentials that vanish at \(Q\).  Outside the common zero locus of a
   184	  basis of this latter space,
   185	  adding \(Q\) lowers \(h^1\) by exactly one.  Starting with the zero
   186	  divisor, for which \(h^1=g\), and repeating this argument \(r\) times
   187	  gives a dense open subset of \(C^r\) on which
   188	  \(h^1(P_1+\cdots+P_r)=g-r\).  Riemann--Roch then gives
   189	  \[
   190	    h^0(P_1+\cdots+P_r)
   191	      =r+1-g+(g-r)=1.
   192	  \]
   193	  Intersecting its finitely many translates under \(S_r\) gives a dense
   194	  symmetric open with the same property.  Its image in the finite quotient
   195	  \(C^{(r)}\) is the complement of the image of its closed invariant
   196	  complement, hence is open and dense.
   197	  Since the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through \(D\) is \(|D|\), it is a single
   198	  point there.
   199	\end{proof}
   200	
   201	\begin{lemma}
   202	  [One-forms pulled back by the Abel--Jacobi map]
   203	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   204	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   205	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   206	
   207	  Pullback by \(\iota_{P_0}\) is an isomorphism
   208	  \[
   209	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0(C,\Omega_C^1).
   210	  \]
   211	\end{lemma}
   212	
   213	\begin{proof}
   214	  \uses{thm:pic0_tangent_space_iso}
   215	  Translation identifies global one-forms on the smooth group scheme \(J\)
   216	  with the cotangent space at its identity.  The tangent-space description
   217	  of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) identifies the tangent space at the identity with
   218	  \(H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\), whose dual is
   219	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\) by Serre duality.  Under these identifications, the
   220	  differential of the moduli class
   221	  \(Q\mapsto[\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0)]\) is the boundary class of the moving
   222	  point; its dual is evaluation of differentials.  Thus the induced map on
   223	  cotangent spaces, and hence the displayed pullback map, is the identity
   224	  under the canonical identifications.
   225	\end{proof}
   226	
   227	\begin{lemma}
   228	  [Dimension of the Jacobian]
   229	  \label{lem:jacobian_dimension}
   230	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107}
   231	
   232	  The Jacobian has dimension \(g\).
   233	\end{lemma}
   234	
   235	\begin{proof}
   236	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms, thm:pic0_smooth}
   237	  Since \(J\) is smooth, its dimension is the dimension of its cotangent
   238	  space at the identity.  Translation identifies that cotangent space with
   239	  the global one-forms on \(J\).  By
   240	  \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, this space is isomorphic to
   241	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), whose dimension is the genus \(g\).
   242	\end{proof}
   243	
   244	\begin{proposition}
   245	  [Differentials on a symmetric power]
   246	  \label{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   247	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   248	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve,
   249	    def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   250	
   251	  Pullback by \(f^{(r)}\) is an isomorphism
   252	  \[
   253	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}
   254	    H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega_{C^{(r)}}^1).
   255	  \]
   256	  Under the canonical identification of either side with
   257	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), the form corresponding to \(\omega\) vanishes at
   258	  an effective divisor \(D\) if and only if
   259	  \(\operatorname{div}(\omega)\ge D\).
   260	\end{proposition}
   261	
   262	\begin{proof}
   263	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   264	  A global one-form on \(C^r\) is a sum of pullbacks from the factors.
   265	  Hence the invariant forms are exactly
   266	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\), with \(\omega\in H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\).
   267	  The quotient map \(\pi_r\) is separable, so pullback embeds
   268	  \(H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)\) into this invariant subspace.  The composite
   269	  \[
   270	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\longrightarrow H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)
   271	      \longrightarrow H^0(C^r,\Omega^1)^{S_r}
   272	  \]
   273	  is the pullback by the sum of the \(r\) copies of the Abel--Jacobi map.
   274	  By \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, it sends a form to
   275	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\) and is an isomorphism.  Consequently both arrows
   276	  in the display are isomorphisms.
   277	
   278	  It remains to identify vanishing at a divisor.  First take \(D=rQ\),
   279	  choose a parameter \(X\) at \(Q\), and write
   280	  \(\omega=(a_0+a_1X+\cdots)dX\).  In the completed local ring of
   281	  \(C^{(r)}\) at \(D\), use the elementary symmetric functions
   282	  \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r\) in local parameters
   283	  \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\), and put
   284	  \(\tau_j=\sum_iX_i^j\,dX_i\).  The identities
   285	  \[
   286	    \sigma_m\tau_0-\sigma_{m-1}\tau_1+\cdots+(-1)^m\tau_m
   287	      =d\sigma_{m+1}
   288	      \qquad(0\le m<r)
   289	  \]
   290	  show that \(\tau_0,\ldots,\tau_{r-1}\) form a basis of the cotangent
   291	  module.  The descended form is \(\sum_{j\ge0}a_j\tau_j\), so it
   292	  vanishes at \(D\) exactly when
   293	  \(a_0=\cdots=a_{r-1}=0\), equivalently when
   294	  \(\operatorname{ord}_Q(\omega)\ge r\).  The same calculation in the
   295	  completed local product for
   296	  \(D=\sum_Q n_QQ\) gives the stated criterion.
   297	\end{proof}
   298	
   299	\begin{lemma}
   300	  [Tangent sequence of the canonical symmetric-power map]
   301	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact}
   302	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   303	  \uses{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   304	
   305	  Let \(F=|D|\) be the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through an effective divisor
   306	  \(D\), and put \(a=f^{(r)}(D)\).  The sequence
   307	  \[
   308	    0\longrightarrow T_DF\longrightarrow T_DC^{(r)}
   309	      \xrightarrow{\,d f^{(r)}_D\,}T_aJ
   310	  \]
   311	  is exact.  In particular, if \(h^0(D)=1\), then
   312	  \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is injective.
   313	\end{lemma}
   314	
   315	\begin{proof}
   316	  \uses{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   317	  The first arrow is injective because the fibre is a closed subscheme, and
   318	  its image lies in the kernel because \(f^{(r)}\) is constant on the
   319	  fibre.  By \cref{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}, the annihilator
   320	  in \(T_aJ^\vee\) of the image of \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is
   321	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\).  Serre duality therefore gives
   322	  \[
   323	    \dim\ker(d f^{(r)}_D)=r-g+h^1(D).
   324	  \]
   325	  The fibre \(F\) is the projective space of effective divisors in the
   326	  complete linear system, so it is smooth of dimension \(h^0(D)-1\).
   327	  Thus \(\dim T_DF=\dim|D|=h^0(D)-1\), and Riemann--Roch says

\section{Smoothness of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\)}
\label{sec:pic0_smooth}

By the tangent-space dimension bound for a Noetherian local ring,
\(\dim_0 \Pic^0_{C/k} \le \dim_k \tu T_0 \Pic^0_{C/k} = g\), with
equality if and only if \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) is regular at \(0\). For a
smooth proper curve, this inequality becomes an equality: smoothness
at the identity propagates to smoothness everywhere by
translation, hence \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) is a smooth \(k\)-group scheme of
dimension \(g\).

\paragraph{Proposition 5.3.}
\textit{(a) For all $r \ge 1$, there are canonical isomorphisms}
\[
  \Gamma(C, \Omega^1) \xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;} \Gamma(C^r, \Omega^1)^{S_r}
  \xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;} \Gamma(C^{(r)}, \Omega^1).
\]
\textit{Let $\omega \in \Gamma(C, \Omega^1)$ correspond to
$\omega' \in \Gamma(C^{(r)}, \Omega^1)$; then for any effective divisor $D$
of degree $r$ on $C$, $(\omega) \ge D$ if and only if $\omega'$ has a zero at
$D$.}

\textit{(b) For all $r \ge 1$, the map
$f^{(r)*} \colon \Gamma(J, \Omega^1) \to \Gamma(C^{(r)}, \Omega^1)$ is an

A global 1-form on a product of projective varieties is a sum of global
1-forms on the factors. Therefore
$\Gamma(C^r, \Omega^1) = \bigoplus_i p_i^* \Gamma(C, \Omega^1)$, where the
$p_i$ are the projection maps onto the factors, and so it is clear that the
map $\omega \mapsto \sum p_i^* \omega$ identifies $\Gamma(C, \Omega^1)$ with
$\Gamma(C^r, \Omega^1)^{S_r}$. Because $\pi \colon C^r \to C^{(r)}$ is
separable,
$\pi^* \colon \Gamma(C^{(r)}, \Omega^1) \to \Gamma(C^r, \Omega^1)$ is
injective, and its image is obviously fixed by the action of $S_r$. The
composite map
\[
  \Gamma(J, \Omega^1) \to \Gamma(C^{(r)}, \Omega^1) \hookrightarrow

$f^{r*} \omega = \sum p_i^* \omega'$. As $f^r = \sum f \circ p_i$, clearly

isomorphisms. It also completes the proof of the proposition except for the
second part of (a), and for this we need a combinatorial lemma.

arising from (2.1). Then (5.3) shows that $\omega$ is zero on the image of
$T_D(C^{(r)})$ if and only if $(\omega) \ge D$, that is,
$\omega \in \Gamma(C, \Omega^1(-D))$. Therefore the image of $(df^{(r)})_D$
has dimension $g - h^0(\Omega^1(-D)) = g - h^1(D)$, and so its kernel has
dimension $r - g + h^1(D)$. On the other hand, the image of $(di)_D$ has
dimension $|D|$. % [sic: printed "dimension |D|", meaning the dimension of the linear system |D|]
The Riemann-Roch theorem says precisely that these two numbers are equal, and
so completes the proof.

\paragraph{Corollary 5.5.}
\textit{For all $r \le g$, $f^r \colon C^r \to W^r$ has degree $r!$.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
It is the composite of $\pi \colon C^r \to C^{(r)}$ and $f^{(r)}$.
\hfill $\square$

\paragraph{Remark 5.6.}
(a) The theorem shows that $J$ is the unique abelian variety birationally
equivalent to $C^{(g)}$. This observation is the basis of Weil's construction
of the Jacobian. (See \S 7.)

(b) The exact sequence in (5.1b) can be regarded as a geometric statement of
the Riemann-Roch theorem (see especially the end of the proof). In fact it is
possible to prove the Riemann-Roch theorem this way (see Mattuck and Mayer
1963).

(c) As we observed above, the fibre of
$f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)}(k) \to J(k)$ containing $D$ can be identified with
the linear system $|D|$. More precisely, the fibre of the map of functors
$C^{(r)} \to J$ is the functor $\Div_C^D$ of (3.14); therefore the fibre of
$f^{(r)}$ containing $D$ (in the sense of algebraic spaces) is a copy of
projective space of dimension $h^0(D) - 1$. Corollary 3.10 of Chapter I shows
that conversely every copy of projective space in $C^{(r)}$ is contained in
some fibre of $f^{(r)}$. Consequently, the closed points of the Jacobian can
be identified with the set of maximal subvarieties of $C^{(r)}$ isomorphic to
projective space.

Note that for $r > 2g - 2$, $|D|$ has dimension $r - g$, and so
$(df^{(r)})_D$ is surjective, for all $D$. Therefore $f^{(r)}$ is smooth (see
Hartshorne 1977, III 10.4), and the fibres of $f^{(r)}$ are precisely the
copies of $\mathbb{P}^{r-g}$ contained in $C^{(r)}$. This last observation is
the starting point of Chow's construction of the Jacobian Chow 1954.
% [sic: printed as "the Jacobian Chow 1954." — hyperlinked citation without parentheses]

    70	\section{Symmetric powers and their canonical maps}
    71	\label{sec:albaneseup_symmetric_powers}
    72	
    73	\begin{definition}
    74	  [Symmetric power of a curve]
    75	  \label{def:symmetric_power_curve}
    76	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0100}
    77	
    78	  For \(r\ge 1\), the \emph{\(r\)-th symmetric power} \(C^{(r)}\) is the
    79	  quotient of \(C^r\) by permutation of the factors, with quotient morphism
    80	  \(\pi_r\colon C^r\to C^{(r)}\).  Every symmetric morphism from \(C^r\) to a
    81	  \(k\)-scheme factors uniquely through \(\pi_r\).
    82	\end{definition}
    83	
    84	\begin{lemma}
    85	  [Properties of the symmetric-power projection]
    86	  \label{lem:symmetric_power_projection_properties}
    87	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0100}
    88	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
    89	
    90	  The quotient morphism \(\pi_r\colon C^r\to C^{(r)}\) is finite,
    91	  surjective, and separable.
    92	\end{lemma}
    93	
    94	\begin{proof}
    95	  On an invariant affine chart the target ring is the ring of
    96	  \(S_r\)-invariants.  Every element of the source ring is integral over this
    97	  invariant ring, so the quotient is finite; the topological quotient
    98	  description gives surjectivity.  Finally, the induced extension of
    99	  function fields is the finite invariant-field extension for a group of
   100	  automorphisms, and is therefore separable.
   101	\end{proof}
   102	
   103	\begin{definition}
   104	  [The symmetric-power carrier]
   105	  \label{def:symmetric_power_curve_carrier}
   106	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.SymmetricPower}
   107	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   108	
   109	  The underlying \(k\)-scheme of \(C^{(r)}\) is denoted
   110	  \(\operatorname{SymmetricPower}(C,r)\).
   111	\end{definition}
   112	
   113	\begin{lemma}
   114	  [Nonsingularity of a symmetric power of a curve]
   115	  \label{lem:symmetric_power_nonsingular}
   116	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0100}
   117	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   118	
   119	  If \(C\) is nonsingular, then \(C^{(r)}\) is nonsingular.
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	
   122	\begin{proof}
   123	  At the image of \((Q,\ldots,Q)\), choose a parameter \(X\) at \(Q\).
   124	  The completed local ring of \(C^r\) is
   125	  \(k[[X_1,\ldots,X_r]]\), and the completed local ring of the quotient is
   126	  its invariant subring.  The fundamental theorem on symmetric functions
   127	  identifies this with
   128	  \(k[[\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r]]\), which is regular.  At a divisor with
   129	  several distinct support points, the completed local ring is the
   130	  completed tensor product of the corresponding invariant power-series
   131	  rings, and is again regular.
   132	\end{proof}
   133	
   134	\begin{definition}
   135	  [The symmetric sum morphism]
   136	  \label{def:symmetric_product_av_map}
   137	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerAVMap}
   138	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve_carrier}
   139	
   140	  For a morphism \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) to an abelian variety, denote the
   141	  induced morphism from the symmetric-power carrier by
   142	  \(\varphi^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\to A\).
   143	\end{definition}
   144	
   145	\begin{lemma}
   146	  [Symmetrisation of a morphism to an abelian variety]
   147	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_av_map}
   148	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   149	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve, def:symmetric_product_av_map}
   150	
   151	  Let \(A\) be an abelian variety and let \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) be a
   152	  morphism.  There is a unique morphism
   153	  \(\varphi^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\to A\) satisfying
   154	  \[
   155	    \varphi^{(r)}(P_1+\cdots+P_r)
   156	      =\varphi(P_1)+\cdots+\varphi(P_r).
   157	  \]
   158	\end{lemma}
   159	
   160	\begin{proof}
   161	  The morphism \(C^r\to A\) obtained by applying \(\varphi\) in every
   162	  coordinate and then adding is invariant under every permutation, because
   163	  the group law of \(A\) is commutative.  The universal property of
   164	  \(C^{(r)}\) gives the unique factorisation.
   165	\end{proof}
   166	
   167	\begin{definition}
   168	  [The canonical symmetric-power morphism to the Jacobian]
   169	  \label{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   170	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107}
   171	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerToJacobian}
   172	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism, def:symmetric_product_av_map}
   173	
   174	  The Lean construction obtained by symmetrising \(\iota_{P_0}\) is denoted
   175	  \[
   176	    f^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\longrightarrow J.
   177	  \]
   178	\end{definition}
   179	
   180	\begin{lemma}
   181	  [Divisor description of the canonical symmetric-power morphism]
   182	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula}
   183	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   184	  \uses{def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism,
   185	    lem:abel_jacobi_morphism, lem:symmetric_product_av_map}
   186	
   187	  On effective divisors, the canonical morphism is given by
   188	  \[
   189	    f^{(r)}(D)=[\mathcal O_C(D-rP_0)].
   190	  \]
   191	  Denote its scheme-theoretic image by \(W^r\).  The fibre through an
   192	  effective divisor \(D\) is its complete linear system \(|D|\), a projective
   193	  space of dimension \(h^0(D)-1\).
   194	\end{lemma}
   195	
   196	\begin{proof}
   197	  Pulling back along \(\pi_r\) gives the sum of the \(r\) Abel--Jacobi
   198	  classes, hence the displayed divisor class.  Two effective divisors have
   199	  the same class precisely when they are linearly equivalent.  The functor
   200	  of effective divisors linearly equivalent to \(D\) is represented by the
   201	  projectivisation of \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(D))\), giving the fibre statement.
   202	\end{proof}
   203	
   204	\begin{lemma}
   205	  [General divisors of degree at most the genus]
   206	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_general_divisor}
   207	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   208	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula}
   209	
   210	  If \(1\le r\le g\), there is a dense open subset of \(C^{(r)}\) on which
   211	  \(h^0(D)=1\).  Thus the fibres of \(f^{(r)}\) over this open consist of one
   212	  geometric point.
   213	\end{lemma}
   214	
   215	\begin{proof}
   216	  \uses{lem:symmetric_power_projection_properties,
   217	    thm:adelic_serreDuality, thm:adelic_riemannRoch}
   218	  If \(h^1(D)>0\), Serre duality identifies
   219	  \[
   220	    H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(D+Q))^\vee
   221	  \]
   222	  with the subspace of \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\) consisting of
   223	  differentials that vanish at \(Q\).  Outside the common zero locus of a
   224	  basis of this latter space,
   225	  adding \(Q\) lowers \(h^1\) by exactly one.  Starting with the zero
   226	  divisor, for which \(h^1=g\), and repeating this argument \(r\) times
   227	  gives a dense open subset of \(C^r\) on which
   228	  \(h^1(P_1+\cdots+P_r)=g-r\).  Riemann--Roch then gives
   229	  \[
   230	    h^0(P_1+\cdots+P_r)
   231	      =r+1-g+(g-r)=1.
   232	  \]
   233	  Intersecting its finitely many translates under \(S_r\) gives a dense
   234	  symmetric open with the same property.  Its image in the finite quotient
   235	  \(C^{(r)}\) is the complement of the image of its closed invariant
   236	  complement, hence is open and dense.
   237	  Since the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through \(D\) is \(|D|\), it is a single
   238	  point there.
   239	\end{proof}
   240	
   241	\begin{lemma}
   242	  [Invariant one-forms on the Jacobian]
   243	  \label{lem:jacobian_invariant_one_forms}
   244	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   245	
   246	  Evaluation at the identity is an isomorphism
   247	  \[
   248	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}T_0J^\vee.
   249	  \]
   250	\end{lemma}
   251	
   252	\begin{proof}
   253	  \uses{thm:pic0_smooth, thm:pic0_proper, thm:pic0_geom_irred}
   254	  A cotangent vector at the identity extends uniquely to a
   255	  translation-invariant one-form on the smooth group scheme \(J\).  Conversely,
   256	  for a global one-form \(\eta\), the coefficients of
   257	  \(t_a^*\eta-\eta\), expressed in an invariant frame, vary regularly with
   258	  \(a\in J\).  They are regular functions on the proper geometrically
   259	  irreducible variety \(J\), hence constant; at \(a=0\) they vanish.  Thus
   260	  every global one-form is invariant, and evaluation at the identity gives
   261	  the asserted inverse pair.
   262	\end{proof}
   263	
   264	\begin{lemma}
   265	  [Differential of the Abel--Jacobi map]
   266	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_differential}
   267	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   268	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   269	
   270	  Under the tangent-space identification
   271	  \(T_0J\simeq H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\) and Serre duality, the transpose of the
   272	  translated differential of \(\iota_{P_0}\) at \(Q\) is evaluation
   273	  \[
   274	    H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\longrightarrow T_Q^*C,
   275	    \qquad \omega\longmapsto\omega(Q).
   276	  \]
   277	\end{lemma}
   278	
   279	\begin{proof}
   280	  \uses{thm:pic0_tangent_space_iso, thm:adelic_serreDuality}
   281	  Moving \(Q\) to first order changes the class
   282	  \([\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0)]\) by the connecting homomorphism associated with
   283	  the principal-parts sequence at \(Q\).  The Serre-duality transpose of
   284	  this connecting homomorphism is the restriction of a differential to its
   285	  value at \(Q\), which is the displayed evaluation map.
   286	\end{proof}
   287	
   288	\begin{lemma}
   289	  [One-forms pulled back by the Abel--Jacobi map]
   290	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   291	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   292	  \uses{lem:jacobian_invariant_one_forms,
   293	    lem:abel_jacobi_differential}
   294	
   295	  Pullback by \(\iota_{P_0}\) is an isomorphism
   296	  \[
   297	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0(C,\Omega_C^1).
   298	  \]
   299	\end{lemma}
   300	
   301	\begin{proof}
   302	  By \cref{lem:jacobian_invariant_one_forms}, a form on \(J\) is determined
   303	  by its value at the identity.  Under
   304	  \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_differential}, pulling it back along
   305	  \(\iota_{P_0}\) recovers at every \(Q\) the corresponding canonical
   306	  differential on \(C\).  Under the Serre-duality identification this map
   307	  is the identity, hence an isomorphism.
   308	\end{proof}
   309	
   310	\begin{lemma}
   311	  [Dimension of the Jacobian]
   312	  \label{lem:jacobian_dimension}
   313	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108}
   314	
   315	  The Jacobian has dimension \(g\).
   316	\end{lemma}
   317	
   318	\begin{proof}
   319	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms, thm:pic0_smooth}
   320	  Since \(J\) is smooth, its dimension is the dimension of its cotangent
   321	  space at the identity.  Translation identifies that cotangent space with
   322	  the global one-forms on \(J\).  By
   323	  \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, this space is isomorphic to
   324	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), whose dimension is the genus \(g\).
   325	\end{proof}
   326	
   327	\begin{proposition}
   328	  [Differentials on a symmetric power]
   329	  \label{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}
   330	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0108, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   331	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula}
   332	
   333	  Pullback by \(f^{(r)}\) is an isomorphism
   334	  \[
   335	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\xrightarrow{\sim}
   336	    H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega_{C^{(r)}}^1).
   337	  \]
   338	  Under the canonical identification of either side with
   339	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\), the form corresponding to \(\omega\) vanishes at
   340	  an effective divisor \(D\) if and only if
   341	  \(\operatorname{div}(\omega)\ge D\).
   342	\end{proposition}
   343	
   344	\begin{proof}
   345	  \uses{lem:symmetric_power_projection_properties,
   346	    lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}
   347	  A global one-form on \(C^r\) is a sum of pullbacks from the factors.
   348	  Hence the invariant forms are exactly
   349	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\), with \(\omega\in H^0(C,\Omega_C^1)\).
   350	  The quotient map \(\pi_r\) is separable, so pullback embeds
   351	  \(H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)\) into this invariant subspace.  The composite
   352	  \[
   353	    H^0(J,\Omega_J^1)\longrightarrow H^0(C^{(r)},\Omega^1)
   354	      \longrightarrow H^0(C^r,\Omega^1)^{S_r}
   355	  \]
   356	  is the pullback by the sum of the \(r\) copies of the Abel--Jacobi map.
   357	  By \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_one_forms}, it sends a form to
   358	  \(\sum_i p_i^*\omega\) and is an isomorphism.  Consequently both arrows
   359	  in the display are isomorphisms.
   360	
   361	  It remains to identify vanishing at a divisor.  First take \(D=rQ\),
   362	  choose a parameter \(X\) at \(Q\), and write
   363	  \(\omega=(a_0+a_1X+\cdots)dX\).  In the completed local ring of
   364	  \(C^{(r)}\) at \(D\), use the elementary symmetric functions
   365	  \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r\) in local parameters
   366	  \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\), and put
   367	  \(\tau_j=\sum_iX_i^j\,dX_i\).  The identities
   368	  \[
   369	    \sigma_m\tau_0-\sigma_{m-1}\tau_1+\cdots+(-1)^m\tau_m
   370	      =d\sigma_{m+1}
   371	      \qquad(0\le m<r)
   372	  \]
   373	  show that \(\tau_0,\ldots,\tau_{r-1}\) form a basis of the cotangent
   374	  module.  The descended form is \(\sum_{j\ge0}a_j\tau_j\), so it
   375	  vanishes at \(D\) exactly when
   376	  \(a_0=\cdots=a_{r-1}=0\), equivalently when
   377	  \(\operatorname{ord}_Q(\omega)\ge r\).  The same calculation in the
   378	  completed local product for
   379	  \(D=\sum_Q n_QQ\) gives the stated criterion.
   380	\end{proof}
   381	
   382	\begin{lemma}
   383	  [Tangent sequence of the canonical symmetric-power map]
   384	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact}
   385	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   386	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula}
   387	
   388	  Let \(F=|D|\) be the fibre of \(f^{(r)}\) through an effective divisor
   389	  \(D\), and put \(a=f^{(r)}(D)\).  The sequence
   390	  \[
   391	    0\longrightarrow T_DF\longrightarrow T_DC^{(r)}
   392	      \xrightarrow{\,d f^{(r)}_D\,}T_aJ
   393	  \]
   394	  is exact.  In particular, if \(h^0(D)=1\), then
   395	  \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is injective.
   396	\end{lemma}
   397	
   398	\begin{proof}
   399	  \uses{prop:symmetric_product_differentials,
   400	    lem:symmetric_power_nonsingular, thm:adelic_serreDuality,
   401	    thm:adelic_riemannRoch}
   402	  The first arrow is injective because the fibre is a closed subscheme, and
   403	  its image lies in the kernel because \(f^{(r)}\) is constant on the
   404	  fibre.  By \cref{prop:symmetric_product_differentials}, the annihilator
   405	  in \(T_aJ^\vee\) of the image of \(d f^{(r)}_D\) is
   406	  \(H^0(C,\Omega_C^1(-D))\).  Serre duality therefore gives
   407	  \[
   408	    \dim\ker(d f^{(r)}_D)=r-g+h^1(D).
   409	  \]
   410	  The fibre \(F\) is the projective space of effective divisors in the
   411	  complete linear system, so it is smooth of dimension \(h^0(D)-1\).
   412	  Thus \(\dim T_DF=\dim|D|=h^0(D)-1\), and Riemann--Roch says
   413	  \(h^0(D)-1=r-g+h^1(D)\).  The included subspaces have the same
   414	  dimension, proving exactness.  When \(h^0(D)=1\), this dimension is zero.
   415	\end{proof}
   416	
   417	\begin{lemma}
   418	  [Birationality of the canonical map]
   419	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}
   420	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0107, abelian-varieties:page-0108,
   421	    abelian-varieties:page-0109}
   422	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula}
   423	
   424	  For \(1\le r\le g\), the morphism
   425	  \[
   426	    f^{(r)}\colon C^{(r)}\longrightarrow W^r
   427	  \]
   428	  is birational.  In particular, \(W^g=J\), and
   429	  \(f^{(g)}\colon C^{(g)}\to J\) is a birational surjective morphism.
   430	\end{lemma}
   431	
   432	\begin{proof}
   433	  \uses{lem:symmetric_power_projection_properties,
   434	    lem:symmetric_product_general_divisor,
   435	    lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact, lem:jacobian_dimension,
   436	    thm:pic0_geom_irred}
   437	  The product \(C^r\) has dimension \(r\), and the finite surjective map
   438	  \(C^r\to C^{(r)}\) shows that \(C^{(r)}\) also has dimension \(r\).
   439	  By \cref{lem:symmetric_product_general_divisor}, the map is injective on
   440	  geometric points over a dense open subset.  It is therefore generically
   441	  quasi-finite, so its image \(W^r\) has dimension \(r\).  Thus the induced extension
   442	  of function fields has separable degree one.  In positive characteristic
   443	  this still leaves open the possibility of a nontrivial purely
   444	  inseparable extension.  Choose \(D\) in that open.  Then \(h^0(D)=1\),
   445	  so \cref{lem:symmetric_product_tangent_exact} makes
   446	  \(d f^{(r)}_D\) injective.  Since source and image both have dimension
   447	  \(r\), the differential has full rank, and the function-field extension
   448	  is generically separable.  Its inseparable degree is therefore also one.
   449	  The function fields of \(C^{(r)}\) and \(W^r\) are equal, proving
   450	  birationality.
   451	
   452	  For \(r=g\), the image \(W^g\) is a closed irreducible subvariety of the
   453	  irreducible variety \(J\) and has dimension \(g=\dim J\), the latter
   454	  equality being \cref{lem:jacobian_dimension}.  Hence
   455	  \(W^g=J\).  Surjectivity follows because \(C^{(g)}\) is proper and its
   456	  image is exactly \(W^g\).
   457	\end{proof}
   458	
   459	\section{Descent and the universal property}
   460	\label{sec:albaneseup_descent}
   461	
   462	\begin{lemma}
   463	  [Descent through the birational symmetric power]
   464	  \label{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma}
   465	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   466	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.descentThroughBirationalSigma}
   467	  \uses{def:symmetric_product_av_map,
   468	    def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   469	
   470	  Let \(A\) be an abelian variety and let
   471	  \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) be pointed at \(P_0\).  There is a unique
   472	  regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\) such that
   473	  \[
   474	    \varphi^{(g)}=\psi\circ f^{(g)}.
   475	  \]
   476	\end{lemma}
   477	
   478	\begin{proof}
   479	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_av_map, lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian,
   480	    lem:symmetric_power_nonsingular, thm:pic0_smooth,
   481	    thm:rational_map_to_av_extends}
   482	  On dense opens \(U\subseteq C^{(g)}\) and \(V\subseteq J\), the map
   483	  \(f^{(g)}|_U\colon U\to V\) is an isomorphism.  Thus
   484	  \(\varphi^{(g)}|_U\circ(f^{(g)}|_U)^{-1}\) defines a rational map
   485	  \(J\dashrightarrow A\).  The Jacobian is smooth and \(A\) is an abelian
   486	  variety, so \cref{thm:rational_map_to_av_extends} extends this rational
   487	  map uniquely to a regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\).  The two
   488	  morphisms \(\varphi^{(g)}\) and \(\psi\circ f^{(g)}\) agree on the dense
   489	  open \(U\); since \(C^{(g)}\) is nonsingular by
   490	  \cref{lem:symmetric_power_nonsingular}, hence reduced, and \(A\) is separated, they
   491	  agree everywhere.  The same dense-open agreement proves uniqueness.
   492	\end{proof}
   493	
   494	\begin{definition}
   495	  [The basepoint section of the symmetric power]
   496	  \label{def:basepoint_section_symmetric_power}
   497	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   498	
   499	  Define
   500	  \[
   501	    s_{P_0}\colon C\longrightarrow C^{(g)},\qquad
   502	    Q\longmapsto Q+(g-1)P_0.
   503	  \]
   504	\end{definition}
   505	
   506	\begin{lemma}
   507	  [The basepoint section followed by the canonical map]
   508	  \label{lem:basepoint_section_to_jacobian}
   509	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   510	  \uses{def:basepoint_section_symmetric_power,
   511	    lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula,
   512	    def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   513	
   514	  One has \(f^{(g)}\circ s_{P_0}=\iota_{P_0}\).
   515	\end{lemma}
   516	
   517	\begin{proof}
   518	  At \(Q\in C\), the left side represents
   519	  \[
   520	    \mathcal O_C(Q+(g-1)P_0-gP_0)=\mathcal O_C(Q-P_0),
   521	  \]
   522	  which is the defining class of \(\iota_{P_0}(Q)\).
   523	\end{proof}
   524	
   525	\begin{lemma}
   526	  [The basepoint section followed by a symmetric sum]
   527	  \label{lem:basepoint_section_symmetric_map}
   528	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   529	  \uses{def:basepoint_section_symmetric_power,
   530	    lem:symmetric_product_av_map}
   531	
   532	  If \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\), then
   533	  \(\varphi^{(g)}\circ s_{P_0}=\varphi\).
   534	\end{lemma}
   535	
   536	\begin{proof}
   537	  At \(Q\in C\), the left side is
   538	  \(\varphi(Q)+(g-1)\varphi(P_0)=\varphi(Q)\).
   539	\end{proof}
   540	
   541	\begin{lemma}
   542	  [Equivalence of the two factorisation equations]
   543	  \label{lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}
   544	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   545	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}
   546	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism, def:symmetric_product_av_map,
   547	    def:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_morphism}
   548	
   549	  Let \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) satisfy \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\).  For every
   550	  regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\),
   551	  \[
   552	    \varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}
   553	      \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   554	    \varphi^{(g)}=\psi\circ f^{(g)}.
   555	  \]
   556	\end{lemma}
   557	
   558	\begin{proof}
   559	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism, lem:symmetric_product_av_map,
   560	    lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian_formula,
   561	    lem:av_regular_map_is_hom, lem:basepoint_section_to_jacobian,
   562	    lem:basepoint_section_symmetric_map}
   563	  Suppose first that \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).  Evaluating at
   564	  \(P_0\) gives \(\psi(0_J)=0_A\), so
   565	  \cref{lem:av_regular_map_is_hom} shows that \(\psi\) is a homomorphism.
   566	  Pulling both sides of the desired symmetric-power equation back to
   567	  \(C^g\), both send \((P_1,\ldots,P_g)\) to
   568	  \(\sum_i\psi(\iota_{P_0}(P_i))\).  The uniqueness clause in the
   569	  universal property of \(C^{(g)}\) gives the equation on \(C^{(g)}\).
   570	
   571	  Conversely, compose the symmetric-power equation with
   572	  \(s_{P_0}\).  The two basepoint-section identities
   573	  \cref{lem:basepoint_section_symmetric_map} and
   574	  \cref{lem:basepoint_section_to_jacobian} identify the resulting equation with
   575	  \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).  Hence
   576	  \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).
   577	\end{proof}
   578	
   579	\begin{theorem}
   580	  [Albanese factorisation through \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\)]
   581	  \label{thm:albanese_universal_property}
   582	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   583	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.albanese_universal_property}
   584	  \uses{def:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   585	
   586	  For every abelian variety \(A\) and every morphism
   587	  \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) with \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\), there exists a unique
   588	  regular morphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\) such that
   589	  \[
   590	    \varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}.
   591	  \]
   592	\end{theorem}
   593	
   594	\begin{proof}
   595	  \uses{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma,
   596	    lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}
   597	  By \cref{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma}, there is a unique
   598	  \(\psi\colon J\to A\) satisfying
   599	  \(\varphi^{(g)}=\psi\circ f^{(g)}\).  The equivalence in
   600	  \cref{lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq}, applied to every candidate
   601	  morphism, transports both existence and uniqueness to the equation
   602	  \(\varphi=\psi\circ\iota_{P_0}\).
   603	\end{proof}
   604	
   605	\begin{corollary}
   606	  [Albanese universal property]
   607	  \label{cor:albanese_universal_property_homomorphism}
   608	  \source{abelian-varieties:page-0110}
   609	  \uses{thm:albanese_universal_property}
   610	
   611	  In the situation of \cref{thm:albanese_universal_property}, the unique
   612	  factor \(\psi\colon J\to A\) is a homomorphism of group schemes.
   613	  Consequently \(\iota_{P_0}\) is initial among pointed morphisms from
   614	  \(C\) to abelian varieties.
   615	\end{corollary}
   616	
   617	\begin{proof}
   618	  \uses{lem:av_regular_map_is_hom, lem:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   619	  Since \(\iota_{P_0}(P_0)=0_J\) and \(\varphi(P_0)=0_A\), the
   620	  factorisation gives \(\psi(0_J)=0_A\).  The pointed rigidity theorem
   621	  \cref{lem:av_regular_map_is_hom} therefore makes \(\psi\) a group
   622	  homomorphism.  Uniqueness among all regular factors implies uniqueness
   623	  among homomorphisms.
   624	\end{proof}

+\section*{3 \quad The symmetric powers of a curve}
+
+Both in order to understand the structure of the Jacobian, and as an aid in
+its construction, we shall need to study the symmetric powers of $C$.
+
+For any variety $V$, the symmetric group $S_r$ on $r$ letters acts on the
+product of $r$ copies $V^r$ of $V$ by permuting the factors, and we want to
+define the $r$th symmetric power $V^{(r)}$ of $V$ to be the quotient
+$S_r \backslash V^r$. The next proposition demonstrates the existence of
+$V^{(r)}$ and lists its main properties.
+
+A morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ is said to be \textit{symmetric} if
+$\varphi\sigma = \varphi$ for all $\sigma$ in $S_r$.
+
+\paragraph{Proposition 3.1.}
+\textit{Let $V$ be a variety over $k$. Then there exists a variety $V^{(r)}$
+and a symmetric morphism $\pi \colon V^r \to V^{(r)}$ having the following
+properties:}
+
+\begin{enumerate}
+\item[(a)] \textit{as a topological space, $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is the quotient
+of $V^r$ by $S_r$;}
+\item[(b)] \textit{for any open affine subset $U$ of $V$, $U^{(r)}$ is an
+open affine subset of $V^{(r)}$ and}
+\[
+  \Gamma(U^{(r)}, \mathcal{O}_{V^{(r)}})
+  = \Gamma(U^r, \mathcal{O}_{V^r})^{S_r}
+\]
+\textit{(set of elements fixed by the action of $S_r$).}
+\end{enumerate}
+
+\textit{The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ has the following universal property:
+every symmetric $k$-morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ factors uniquely
+through $\pi$.}
+
+\textit{The map $\pi$ is finite, surjective, and separable.}
+
+\paragraph{Proof.}
+If $V$ is affine, say $V = \operatorname{Specm}(A)$, define $V^{(r)}$ to be
+$\operatorname{Specm}((A \otimes_k \cdots \otimes_k A)^{S_r})$. In the
+general case, write $V$ as a union $\bigcup U_i$ of open affines, and construct
+% [sic: printed "construct V"; the context requires "construct V^{(r)}".]
+$V$ by patching together the $U_i^{(r)}$. See Mumford 1970, II, \S 7, p66,
+and III, \S 11, p112, for the details. \hfill $\square$
+
+The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is uniquely determined up to a unique isomorphism
+by its universal property. It is called the $r$th \textit{symmetric power} of
+$V$.
+
+\paragraph{Proposition 3.2.}
+\textit{The symmetric power $C^{(r)}$ of a nonsingular curve is nonsingular.}
+
+\paragraph{Proof.}
+We may assume that $k$ is algebraically closed. The most likely candidate for
+a singular point on $C^{(r)}$ is the image $Q$ of a fixed point
+$(P, \ldots, P)$ of $S_r$ on $C^r$, where $P$ is a closed point of $C$. The
+completion $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_P$ of the local ring at $P$ is isomorphic to
+$k[[X]]$, and so
+\[
+  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{(P,\ldots,P)}
+  \approx k[[X]] \widehat{\otimes} \cdots \widehat{\otimes} k[[X]]
+  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]].
+\]
+It follows that
+$\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r}$, where $S_r$
+acts by permuting the variables. The fundamental theorem on symmetric
+functions says that, over any ring, a symmetric polynomial can be expressed
+as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions
+$\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r$. This implies that
+\[
+  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r} = k[[\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r]],
+\]
+which is regular, and so $Q$ is nonsingular.
+
+For a general point $Q = \pi(P, P, \ldots, P', \ldots)$ with $P$ occurring
+$r'$ times, $P'$ occurring $r''$ times, and so on,
+\[
+  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q
+  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r'}]]^{S_{r'}} \widehat{\otimes}
+  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r''}]]^{S_{r''}} \widehat{\otimes} \cdots,
+\]
+which the same argument shows to be regular. \hfill $\square$
